questions.q: Why doesn't Oracle have separate sized integer types like SQL Server's INT, BIGINT, and SMALLINT?
options: Oracle uses one general-purpose NUMBER type, and its INTEGER keyword is simply an alias for NUMBER(38)
Oracle does not support integer values at all
Oracle requires every numeric column to be declared as VARCHAR2
Oracle has more sized integer types than SQL Server, not fewer
questions.explain: Oracle doesn't distinguish sized integer types at the storage-declaration level; a migration usually maps to NUMBER with an appropriate precision instead.

questions.q: Which category of data-type mapping does this lesson describe as close to mechanical across all four platforms?
options: Decimal / numeric types, since DECIMAL/NUMERIC/NUMBER(p,s) all behave the same way conceptually with explicit precision and scale
Boolean types, since all four platforms have an identical native boolean
Date/datetime types, since all four handle time components identically
String types, since Unicode handling is identical everywhere
questions.explain: Fixed-precision numeric types are one of the few mappings that translate cleanly without real judgment calls.

questions.q: Why might Oracle's plain DATE type be the right target for a SQL Server DATETIME2 column, according to this lesson?
options: Oracle's DATE type actually includes a time component down to the second, unlike SQL Server's date-only DATE
Oracle's DATE type cannot store any time information at all, same as SQL Server's DATE
Oracle has no DATE type, only TIMESTAMP
SQL Server's DATETIME2 never includes a time value
questions.explain: This is a genuine quirk worth knowing: Oracle's DATE is not date-only the way SQL Server's DATE is.

questions.q: Which platform is the only one of the four described as having a genuine native BOOLEAN type?
options: PostgreSQL
SQL Server
MySQL
Oracle, in every version
questions.explain: SQL Server uses BIT, MySQL's BOOLEAN is an alias for TINYINT(1), and Oracle traditionally has no native boolean column type before 23c.

questions.q: What are the two realistic conventions for representing a boolean value on a pre-23c Oracle target, per this lesson?
options: NUMBER(1) storing 0/1, or CHAR(1) storing 'Y'/'N'
A native BOOLEAN type identical to PostgreSQL's
TINYINT(1), the same alias MySQL uses
Oracle cannot store boolean-like values in any form
questions.explain: Pre-23c Oracle has no native boolean type, so a migration has to pick one of these long-standing conventions and apply it consistently.
